sources.note: A construction-industry blog, not a primary trade-association or government source, but specific and directly on point: states that angled layouts, curved walls, and specialty architectural features add 30-60% to baseline framing costs versus simple rectangular buildings, attributed to the extra cutting, custom fabrication, and specialized layout non-repeated members require. This case's MA3 (45% premium) is the case author's own point estimate anchored inside this sourced range, not the range itself presented as a hard fact -- no public per-cut timing study exists for hip-rafter fabrication specifically.

sources.title: How Much Does Land Grading Cost?
sources.note: A home-services cost-guide aggregator, not a primary source. Corrected 2026-09-05 after a direct re-fetch: the page's own headline range is 0.08-2.00 dollars per sq ft overall, but it breaks this into fine/finish grading (0.40-1.00 dollars/sq ft, leveling the top 1-3in of soil) and rough grading (1.00-2.00 dollars/sq ft, removing slopes or contouring for drainage). This case anchors MA4 (Option A, more full-envelope regrading -- rough-grading category) and MA5 (Option B, lighter finish grading only -- fine-grading category) inside their respective, more specific sub-ranges, not the vague overall headline figure.

deliverables.text: A labeled plan-view sketch of each frame option, correctly identified as a regular octagon (Option A) or an irregular hexagon (Option B), with every vertex marked.

Using the sum of the interior angles of a polygon theorem, find every interior angle of both options -- Option A via regular-polygon congruence, Option B via the theorem plus the five known corner angles to find the sixth -- then state and justify whether each frame is convex.

For each option, compute the hip-rafter run, rise, and length at every vertex using the roof pitch and the Pythagorean theorem, showing why Option A's eight hips come out identical while Option B's six do not.
Identify the quadrilateral shape formed by one roof panel in each option and classify it as specifically as the evidence allows, justified from which sides/angles are or are not congruent.
Full framing takeoff: hip-rafter length, board-feet, material cost, fabrication labor cost, site-prep cost, and covered square feet per dollar for each option; state the winner and margin.

balance.argument_a: The Even Eight's eight identical hip rafters mean a single pattern cut is batch-repeated 8 times (Appendix E MA2), holding fabrication labor to $38.83 and total board length to 195.70 ft ($102.03 material) -- and while its symmetric shape must clear the buildable envelope's tightest corner, capping its covered footprint at 477.17 sq ft, its total frame-plus-site-prep cost of $665.74 is a real, independently defensible number built entirely from repeated, low-risk shop operations. On the twist's own different metric -- total shop setup-and-cut time -- The Even Eight needs only about 1.58 hours against The Site Six's roughly 3.45 hours, a real advantage when the truss shop's cutoff is what stands between the committee and the matching grant.
balance.argument_b: The Site Six's irregular hexagon captures 510.00 sq ft against The Even Eight's 477.17 -- 6.9% more usable covered space from the same buildable envelope, because it is fit to the envelope's own six corners instead of shrinking to clear the worst one. Even after pricing in the real fabrication premium of six non-identical hip rafters (Appendix E MA3, $42.22 labor vs. $38.83) and its own site-prep mix, its total frame-plus-site-prep cost of $639.02 is lower than The Even Eight's $665.74, and it delivers more square footage per dollar (0.7981 vs. 0.7168) on the case's own graded metric -- a real win, not a paper one, since it holds even after both real fabrication and site-prep costs are fully priced in.
balance.margin_basis: Total covered footprint (sq ft) divided by total frame material + fabrication labor + site-prep cost (USD) for each option, computed in cases/the-bandstand-angle/sensitivity_model.py evaluate(PARAMS) from Appendix B/C/E figures.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The corner lot's buildable envelope, both frame options' side lengths and hip-rafter runs, the covered footprint areas, and five of the hexagon's six surveyed interior angles
modeling_assumptions.value_used: See Appendix B for the full figure set
modeling_assumptions.basis: No real property was used. The figures are built to be internally consistent with a real corner-lot infill site with a partially completed re-survey -- a common, realistic situation for a small volunteer-driven public project.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This defines the two frame designs being compared, not an uncertain quantity -- if the sixth corner is later re-staked at a different angle, D2's arithmetic answer changes, but neither option's shape or the case's dilemma changes. Not swept by Tier 2 Probe 5 for this reason.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Time to mark and cut one of Option A's identical hip rafters (a batch cut)
modeling_assumptions.basis: A single-pattern, single-bevel cut repeated down a run of identical pieces -- a fast, well-established shop operation once the first piece is pattern-cut. No public per-cut timing study exists for this specific operation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Time to mark and cut one of Option B's non-identical hip rafters, as a premium over MA2
modeling_assumptions.basis: Each of Option B's six hip rafters needs its own layout and test-fit because none of them share a pattern. Anchored inside the sourced 30-60% range for custom/non-repeated framing labor [S3]. No public per-cut timing study exists for this specific operation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.basis: The Even Eight's symmetric footprint does not track the buildable envelope's existing grade the way a custom-fit shape can, so more of its footprint needs full cut-and-fill regrading, not just surface leveling. Anchored inside the sourced 1.00-2.00 dollars/sq ft ROUGH-grading sub-range [S4].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.basis: The Site Six's vertices were chosen to follow the buildable envelope's existing grade, so only light finish grading is needed. Anchored inside the sourced 0.40-1.00 dollars/sq ft FINE/FINISH-grading sub-range [S4].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

sensitivity_note: The graded primary metric (covered sq ft per dollar of frame + site-prep cost) is sensitive to MA2-MA5. Tier 2 Probe 5 (flexing each +/-50% independently) found MA2 (simple-cut time) and MA3 (custom-cut premium) do NOT flip the verdict or breach the SPEC section 2 20%% cap at either flex extreme. MA4/MA5 (the two site-prep rates) DO: flexing site_prep_rate_a -50%% or site_prep_rate_b +50%% flips the winner to Option A, and every flex of either site-prep rate pushes the margin past the 20%% cap. This is disclosed, not eliminated, per case.json.sensitivity_disclosure[] (Category X -- no real site-prep quote can exist for this constructed, non-real lot; both rates are good-faith point estimates anchored inside the same sourced /bin/zsh.80-.00/sq ft public land-grading range, S4). MA1 (the constructed site geometry) is NOT swept -- it defines the two options being compared, not an uncertain quantity. The twist (FACILITATOR.md) reveals a genuinely different metric -- total shop setup-and-cut time -- on which Option A wins by a wide margin, independent of the graded dollar metric.
